from.place: Proof paragraph 2, finite coefficient mapping-complex adjunction before R lim; supporting the enriched tensor/localization calculus: Lemma 5.1.2, Proposition 5.1.15, Corollaries 5.2.7 and 5.2.10, Lemmas 5.3.2, 5.3.4 and 5.3.5, Proposition 5.3.6; Lemma A.5.5

title: Equivalence nerves and detection of fully faithful equivalences
statement: Let $\mathcal V$ be presentably monoidal, and use the algebroids of [def-coef-complete-algebroid]. For an algebroid $C$ with object space $U(C)$, put $I_n(C)=\operatorname{Map}(E^n,C)$ and $I(C)=|I_\bullet(C)|$, the geometric realization in spaces. The finite sets $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with their usual maps make $E^\bullet$ cosimplicial and $I_\bullet(C)$ simplicial. For a nonempty ordered subset $S\subseteq[n]$, write $I_S(C)=I_{|S|-1}(C)$, with restriction maps induced by its increasing enumeration. There is a natural identification $I_0(C)\simeq U(C)$. The simplicial space $I_\bullet(C)$ is a groupoid object: for every union $[n]=S\cup T$ of ordered subsets meeting in one vertex, restriction identifies $I_n(C)$ with $I_S(C)\times_{I_{S\cap T}(C)}I_T(C)$. The algebroid $C$ is complete if and only if $U(C)\to I(C)$ is an equivalence. A fully faithful $F:C\to D$ induces equivalences on the fibers of $I_1(C)\to U(C)^2$ over $(x,y)$ and $I_1(D)\to U(D)^2$ over $(Fx,Fy)$. An element of the fiber $I_1(C)_{x,y}$ is an equivalence from $x$ to $y$; this fiber identifies with the union of invertible components in $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))$. A functor is essentially surjective if and only if every target object is equivalent to an image object, or equivalently if $\pi_0 I(F)$ is surjective. If it is also fully faithful, then $I(F)$ is an equivalence. A fully faithful algebroid map whose map on object spaces is an equivalence is an equivalence in $\operatorname{Algd}(\mathcal V)$. Composition on either side with an equivalence between objects induces equivalences of enriched mapping objects. All these statements are natural in algebroid maps.

source.place: Lemma 5.1.2, Propositions 5.1.15 and 5.1.17, Corollaries 5.2.7 and 5.2.10, Lemmas 5.3.2, 5.3.4 and 5.3.5, Proposition 5.3.6; Lemma A.5.5 (read online; not archived in literature/). No Stacks tag states this infinity-categorical fact.

proof.text: The finite-set algebroids $E^n$ and their maps are defined in [def-coef-complete-algebroid]. Precomposition reverses the cosimplicial operators and gives the stated simplicial space. The definition of completeness there is exactly that $I_0(C)\to|I_\bullet(C)|$ is an equivalence. Step 5 will identify its evaluation map $I_0(C)\to U(C)$ naturally as an equivalence, which then gives the asserted completeness criterion.

Let $\mathcal T$ be the terminal monoidal category. By [lem-coef-algebroid-segal-localization-model], $P(\mathcal T)=\mathcal S$ is presentably monoidal; its Day tensor is cartesian product. Apply the extension clause of [lem-coef-operadic-day-convolution] to the strong monoidal functor $\mathcal T\to\mathcal V$ selecting the tensor unit with its unit constraints. It gives a colimit-preserving strong monoidal $T:\mathcal S\to\mathcal V$, with $T(*)\simeq\mathbf1$, and its lax monoidal right adjoint $R(v)=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,v)$. This uses the cited monoidal extension theorem, including its coherence, rather than inferring monoidality from an objectwise tensor comparison.

source.place: Example 4.3.20; monoidal Yoneda extension as stated in the cited Day-convolution node.

proof.text: Construct the object-space mapping formula without using equivalence nerves. For either coefficient category $\mathcal B=\mathcal V$ or $\mathcal S$, [def-coef-complete-algebroid] defines the total category of the restriction functor $X\mapsto\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal B)$. Enlarge universes so that the space category and all these fibers are small in the universe to which straightening is applied. Apply [lem-coef-cocartesian-straightening] to $X\mapsto\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal B)^{\mathrm{op}}$ over $\mathcal S^{\mathrm{op}}$, then take opposites. The resulting Cartesian Grothendieck construction is the defined total category: its arrows are exactly pairs $(\phi,A\to\phi^*B)$ with their coherent simplices. Its Cartesian lift to $B$ over $\phi:X\to Y$ is $\phi^*B\to B$, represented by the identity of $\phi^*B$. The opposite, $K=\Delta^0$ case of [lem-coef-infinity-pointwise-cocartesian-transport] therefore identifies the homotopy fiber over $\phi$ of $\operatorname{Map}(A,B)\to\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal S}(X,Y)$ with $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal B)}(A,\phi^*B)$. These comparisons are natural under coefficient postcomposition, which commutes with restriction.

source.place: Lemma 4.3.19, mapping-fiber calculation; straightening and Cartesian mapping-fiber criterion, as stated in the cited nodes.

proof.text:
Postcomposition with $T$ and $R$ gives $T_*$ and $R_*$, with unchanged object spaces and $R_*C(x,y)=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))$. For each $X$, replace $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$ by the small ordinary operad $q(X)=L_{\mathrm{gen}}\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$ using [lem-coef-many-object-operad-accessibility]. The restriction-natural adjunction in [lem-coef-operadic-change-enrichment] gives $T_X\dashv R_X$ on these fibers, with their algebra units, counits and triangle homotopies. Since postcomposition commutes with restriction, $R_*$ preserves the Cartesian lifts of Step 3. Thus $R_*^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a cocartesian-edge-preserving functor over $\mathcal S^{\mathrm{op}}$, and its fiber functors have specified right adjoints $T_X^{\mathrm{op}}$. Apply [lem-coef-cocartesian-relative-right-adjoint] and take opposites. This gives $T_*\dashv R_*$ over $\mathcal S$: the fiber units and counits assemble on the defined total categories because they commute coherently with operad restriction, and their triangle homotopies assemble for the same reason. In particular the left functor is the postcomposition $T_*$, with these algebra transformations, not merely an assignment on fibers. For a nonempty finite set $A$, let $E_A$ denote $E^{|A|-1}$ with its objects relabelled by $A$. Strong monoidality identifies $T_*E_A^{\mathcal S}\simeq E_A^{\mathcal V}$, including units and all finite-set maps. Hence naturally in $A,C$,
$$\operatorname{Map}(E_A^{\mathcal V},C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(E_A^{\mathcal S},R_*C).$$

source.place: Lemma 4.3.19, Example 4.3.20, Definition 5.1.10 and Proposition 5.1.11; restriction-natural fiber adjunction assembled by the cited relative-adjoint theorem.

proof.text: In [lem-coef-algebroid-segal-localization-model], take the small monoidal category to be the terminal category and take the coefficient localization set empty. Then $P(*)=\mathcal S$, its Day tensor is cartesian product (both sides at the only object are the product of values), and $Q_*$ is the full category of Segal spaces. The stated equivalence identifies $R_*C$ with a Segal space $W_C$, with $(W_C)_0=U(C)$ and $(W_C)(x,y)=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))$. Under this same explicit object-and-mapping-object identification, $E_A^{\mathcal S}$ has $(n+1)$-tuples of objects $A^{n+1}$ in degree $n$, with the uniquely prescribed composites: it is $dG_A$ for $G_A=N(\mathcal I_A)$. Full faithfulness of that equivalence now turns Step 4 into $\operatorname{Map}(E_A^{\mathcal V},C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal P_\Delta}(dG_A,W_C)$. These equivalences respect every finite-set map, evaluation on edges, units and composition. For a singleton $A$, $dG_A$ is the constant point simplicial space, which is the free diagram $[0]!*$ on $[0]\in\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, since there is exactly one map $[n]\to[0]$ in $\Delta$. The free-diagram mapping equivalence in [lem-coef-coherent-diagram-coyoneda], with $I=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $\mathcal B=\mathcal S$, gives $\operatorname{Map}(dG_A,W_C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(*,(W_C)_0)\simeq U(C)$. Its map is evaluation at that vertex. Hence $I_0(C)\simeq U(C)$ naturally; applying the Step 1 definition proves the completeness assertion.

source.place: Theorem 4.4.7; the explicit identification of coarse algebras in the proof of Theorem 5.2.5.; evaluation by the free-diagram adjunction (relative Yoneda)

proof.text:
Fix a nonempty finite set $A$, $a\in A$ and $b\notin A$. By [lem-coef-coarse-nerve-gluing], the inclusion $G_A\amalg_{G_{\{a\}}}G_{\{a,b\}}\to G_{A\cup\{b\}}$ is inner anodyne. Apply [lem-coef-segal-space-inner-anodyne-locality] to the Segal space $W_C$ of Step 5. It identifies restriction along this inclusion as an equivalence of mapping spaces. The displayed degreewise pushout also becomes a pushout of simplicial spaces after applying $d$: in each degree both legs are injections of sets, and writing them as $B=A_0\amalg B'$ and $D=A_0\amalg D'$ gives their pushout $A_0\amalg B'\amalg D'$. Mapping these discrete spaces to any space gives the pullback of products with the same decomposition, so this is also a homotopy pushout. Pointwise colimits and the conversion of a colimit into a limit by contravariant mapping spaces are supplied by [lem-coef-infinity-yoneda-presheaf-limits]. Since $G_{\{a\}}$ is the vertex, Step 5 now gives the canonical restriction equivalence
$$\operatorname{Map}(dG_{A\cup\{b\}},W_C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(dG_A,W_C)\times_{(W_C)_0}\operatorname{Map}(dG_{\{a,b\}},W_C).$$

source.place: Theorem 5.2.5, one-vertex attachment, using Haugseng 2311.13362v1 Corollary 6.6 for Segal locality.

proof.text: For $[n]=S\cup T$ with $S\cap T=\{a\}$, induct on the number of vertices of $T\setminus\{a\}$. When $T=\{a\}$ restriction is the identity. For the induction step, attach one new vertex $b$ at the common pivot $a$ and use the restriction equivalence of Step 6. After all attachments it identifies $\operatorname{Map}(dG_{S\cup T},W_C)$ with $\operatorname{Map}(dG_S,W_C)$ times one two-object factor for every vertex of $T\setminus\{a\}$, all over $(W_C)_0$. The same attachments starting with $\{a\}$ identify the product of those two-object factors with $\operatorname{Map}(dG_T,W_C)$. Associativity of the pullback gives $I_n(C)\simeq I_S(C)\times_{I_{S\cap T}(C)}I_T(C)$ by Step 5. Coarse nerves admit all permutations of their labels, so this also holds when the pivot is not an endpoint in the inherited ordering. The canonical comparison is always the stated restriction map; enumeration only proves it is an equivalence.

Apply [lem-coef-segal-inverse-evaluation] to $W_C$. The two-object coarse nerve $G_{\{0,1\}}$ in Step 5 is its walking isomorphism $E$, so evaluation gives $I_1(C)\simeq(W_C)_{\mathrm{inv}}$ over $U(C)^2$. Pull back over $(x,y)$ and use Step 5's identification of the mapping space to obtain the stated union of invertible components of $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))$. A map $E^1\to C$ together with identifications of its endpoints with $(x,y)$ is exactly a point of this homotopy fiber; these endpoint identifications are paths, not strict equalities. Under the coefficient adjunction and Segal comparison, its edge is a map $\mathbf1\to C(x,y)$ invertible in $hW_C$, hence admitting a reverse arrow and both unit homotopies. Conversely Rezk evaluation says that every such invertible edge extends through $E^1$ with a contractible space of coherent choices. Thus these are precisely object equivalences in the enriched category. This proves the assertion for the whole fiber space, not merely a bijection on its components.

source.place: Theorem 6.2, with the invertible-arrow subspace of Sections 5.5 and 5.7; the enriched application is Gepner-Haugseng Propositions 5.1.15 and 5.1.17.

proof.text: Let $F:C\to D$ be fully faithful. Its mapping-object equivalences induce equivalences of spaces $H_C(x,y)=\operatorname{Map}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))\simeq H_D(Fx,Fy)$. They preserve units and compositions, so they preserve invertibility. Conversely, if the image of $\alpha\in H_C(x,y)$ has an inverse, lift this inverse to $\beta\in H_C(y,x)$. The equations for its two composites lift on components through the equivalences $H_C(x,x)\simeq H_D(Fx,Fx)$ and $H_C(y,y)\simeq H_D(Fy,Fy)$, giving $\beta\alpha=1_x$ and $\alpha\beta=1_y$ in the homotopy category. Thus $F$ reflects invertibility as well. Restricting an equivalence of spaces to the corresponding unions of components is an equivalence (it restricts the bijection on components and retains every based homotopy group). Step 8 identifies these restrictions with exactly the required maps on $I_1$ fibers.

source.place: Lemma 5.3.5, with reflection of invertibility checked by lifting a two-sided inverse.

proof.text: By Step 7 and [lem-coef-space-geometric-descent], $I_\bullet(C)$ and $I_\bullet(D)$ are effective groupoids. Thus $U(C)\to I(C)$ and $U(D)\to I(D)$ are surjective on components, and $I_1(D)\simeq U(D)\times_{I(D)}U(D)$. If every object of $D$ is equivalent to an image, each component of $I(D)$ consequently meets the image of $I(C)$. Conversely, if $\pi_0I(F)$ is surjective, lift any target component first to $U(C)$ using its surjection on components. Equality of its image with the component of an object $d$ means a path in $I(D)$ from that image to $d$; effectivity identifies this path with a point of the corresponding $I_1(D)$ fiber, hence with an object equivalence by Step 8. This proves the equivalence between the two formulations; [def-coef-complete-algebroid] defines essential surjectivity by the component formulation.

source.place: Lemma 5.3.4, with the quotient argument expressed using effectivity.

proof.text: Put $A=I(C)$, $B=I(D)$ and $f=I(F)$. Effectivity identifies the path spaces of $A$ between points of $U(C)$ with the corresponding fibers of $I_1(C)$, and similarly for $B$. Hence Step 9 gives equivalences on these path spaces. Apply the final descent criterion of [lem-coef-space-geometric-descent] to the square with top row $A\xrightarrow{f}B$ and bottom row $A\times A\xrightarrow{f\times f}B\times B$, whose vertical maps are diagonals. The map $U(C)^2\to A^2$ is surjective on components; over any of its points the fiber comparison is exactly the path-space equivalence just proved. Descent therefore makes its comparison $A\to A\times_B A$ an equivalence. For any $b\in B$, the homotopy fiber $H$ of $f$ consequently has diagonal $H\to H\times H$ an equivalence. If $F$ is also essentially surjective, Step 10 makes each such $H$ nonempty. Choose $h\in H$; a homotopy inverse to the diagonal gives $\mathrm{pr}_1\simeq\mathrm{pr}_2$ on $H\times H$, and restriction along $z\mapsto(z,h)$ contracts $H$ to $h$. Every fiber of $f$ is therefore contractible, so [lem-coef-space-contractible-fiber-equivalence] implies that $I(F)$ is an equivalence. If $B$ is empty, so is $A$; the same criterion is vacuous and still applies.

source.place: Proposition 5.3.6; the homotopy-monomorphism and surjectivity argument is written out using descent and contractible fibers.

proof.text: Suppose $F:C\to D$ is fully faithful and $f=U(F):X\to Y$ is an equivalence. In the total-category description of [def-coef-complete-algebroid], write $F$ as $C\xrightarrow{\alpha}f^*D\to D$. Its vertical factor $\alpha$ is a map of $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$-algebras with equivalences at all colors $(x,x')$, by full faithfulness. By [lem-coef-many-object-operad-accessibility], $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a generalized nonsymmetric infinity operad, small since $X$ is small, with colors $X^2$. Since $\mathcal V$ is presentably monoidal, the conservativity clause of [lem-coef-operadic-colorwise-sifted-colimits] says that $\alpha$ is an equivalence. The second factor is the Cartesian lift constructed in Step 3. For every testing algebroid $T$, its mapping-space square over $\operatorname{Map}(U(T),X)\to\operatorname{Map}(U(T),Y)$ is a homotopy pullback by the mapping-square clause of [lem-coef-cocartesian-straightening], applied to opposites. The bottom map is an equivalence, hence so is $\operatorname{Map}(T,f^*D)\to\operatorname{Map}(T,D)$. Composing with $\alpha$ gives an equivalence $\operatorname{Map}(T,C)\to\operatorname{Map}(T,D)$. At $T=D$, lift $1_D$ to $G:D\to C$, giving $FG\simeq1_D$. At $T=C$, the images of $GF$ and $1_C$ agree up to homotopy, so the mapping-space equivalence gives $GF\simeq1_C$. These homotopies exhibit $F$ as an equivalence, without completeness.

source.place: Lemma 5.3.2 and its Cartesian mapping-space criterion, equivalent to the conservativity argument of Lemma A.5.5.

proof.text: For an object equivalence $\alpha:x\to y$, Step 8 supplies a reverse arrow $\beta:y\to x$ and the two inverse homotopies. Composition and units are those of the algebroid in [def-coef-complete-algebroid]. Precomposition by $\alpha$ on $C(y,z)\to C(x,z)$ has inverse precomposition by $\beta$; associativity identifies their composites with composition by $\alpha\beta$ or $\beta\alpha$, and the inverse equations and unit homotopies identify these with identity maps of the enriched mapping objects themselves. For postcomposition, let $a:C(z,x)\to C(z,y)$ and $b:C(z,y)\to C(z,x)$ be composition with $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Associativity gives $ba\simeq(\beta\alpha)_*$ and $ab\simeq(\alpha\beta)_*$. The inverse equations $\beta\alpha\simeq1_x$ and $\alpha\beta\simeq1_y$, followed by the unit homotopies, identify these composites with $1_{C(z,x)}$ and $1_{C(z,y)}$. Thus $a$ and $b$ exhibit $C(z,x)\simeq C(z,y)$. This proves the assertion in $\mathcal V$, rather than only after applying $\operatorname{Map}(\mathbf1,-)$.

All identifications used here are induced by evaluation, precomposition with maps of finite coarse categories, the mapping-space adjunction and the canonical pullback comparisons. For an algebroid map $C\to D$, postcomposition commutes with every one of these restrictions; on an arbitrary higher simplex it is the same associative composition of the specified coherent functors. Units, composition and their homotopies are part of an algebroid map. Thus the identifications of simplicial spaces and of invertible-arrow subspaces, the fiber comparisons, and the induced augmentations commute coherently with algebroid maps. The temporary choices of enumerations or inverses in the proof establish equivalences of these canonical maps and do not enter their definitions.

source.place: Naturality of the canonical evaluation and restriction maps throughout Sections 5.1-5.3.

proof_origin.place: Proof paragraph 2: foundational equivalence-nerve calculus along the inherited completion/tensor/localization ancestry.
